1. We heard Ms. Aparna Bhat, the learned Amicus and other learned
counsel appearing for various parties.

Force is preparing its final report. The Task Force would be
finalizing the final report in near future and would place it
before us for our consideration. However, according to the learned
Amicus, the Order passed by this Court dated 27th May, 2026 has not
been complied with by some of the States.

Although the State of Uttarakhand was not mentioned in I.A. No. 95105
of 2026, a subsequent cross-verification undertaken pursuant to the
Order dated 27.05.2026 has revealed that the State has likewise failed
to comply with the directions contained therein. This lapse was duly
communicated to the State authorities, however, the compliance remains
pending till date.
4. The learned counsel appearing for the State of Meghalaya
submitted  that  they  have  furnished  the  necessary  information
required by the Task Force today. If that be so, the learned Amicus
may look into it. 
5. We grant one last opportunity to the States of Himachal
Pradesh, Mizoram, Odisha and Telangana to furnish the required
information. If information is not provided within a period of two
weeks from today, we shall take appropriate steps in accordance
with law for non-compliance of our directions.
6. We direct the State of Uttarakhand also to furnish the
necessary information as required by the Task Force within a period
of two weeks from today.

IA No.209985/2026 – for directions:-
1. Taking into consideration the averments made in the said
application, relief as prayed for is granted. 
2. The Ministry of Education, Government of India shall release
and disburse a sum of Rs.10,00,000/- (Rupees Ten Lakh only) towards
the functioning and operational expenses of the National Task Force
constituted vide Judgment dated 24/03/2025 within a period of one
week from today. 
3. The amount shall be deposited by the Ministry of Education
into the Bank Account of the National Task Force having details as
mentioned in Para 4 of the application.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
JHARKHAND
1. We have perused the affidavit dated 01st August, 2026. It is stated therein
that out of 211 contractual (special teachers) in position, only 33 of them were
found to be eligible having qualification of Jharkhand Teacher Eligibility Test
(JTET).
2. Our  attention  has  been  drawn  by  Mr.  Rishi  Malhotra,  learned  amicus
curiae  to  the  order  dated  07th March,  2025.  It  appears  therefrom  that  the
mandatory  requirement  for  the  contractual  teachers  is  specified  as  RCI
qualification.
3. In such view of the matter, we direct the State of Jharkhand to consider
the claims of the 211 (contractual) special teachers strictly on the terms of the
order dated 07 th March, 2025, without insisting that they should have qualified
the JTET.
4. An appropriate decision shall be taken within two months from date.
5. If  any  one  of  these  211  (contractual)  special  teachers  has  taken  the
14

## Page 95

Jharkhand  Staff  Selection  Commission  (JSSC)  examination,  their  fate  will  be
determined by the exercise to be carried out in terms of the order of 07 th March,
2025 and not by the outcome of the result of the JSSC examination.
6. Insofar as the applicants represented by Mr. Rahul Kaushik, learned senior
counsel are concerned, they having taken the JSSC examination, their fate will
be determined by the result of such examination.
7. The remaining posts may be filled up in accordance with law. 
8. I.A. No.327111/2025 & I.A. No.327075/2025 stand disposed of.
Uttarakhand
9. We have perused the affidavit dated 27 th July, 2026. It appears therefrom
that there are 29 (contractual) special teachers including one Neeraj Kumar (I.A.
No.221639/2025). Of them, 4 have been considered eligible while the remaining
25 (contractual) special teachers have not been considered eligible because
they seem to be lacking TET qualification.
10. We, accordingly, direct the State of Uttarakhand to consider the cases of
these 25 (contractual) special teachers. In the event, they possess the requisite
RCI qualification, they shall be considered for regularisation in terms of the
order dated 07 th March 2025 within two months, notwithstanding the fact that
they do not have TET qualification.
11. The remaining posts may be filled up in accordance with law.
Madhya Pradesh 
12. Mr. Raizada, learned counsel appearing for the State of Madhya Pradesh,
submits that in compliance with the order dated 21 st April, 2026 of this Court, a
15

## Page 96

report in a sealed cover has been filed this month.
13. The said report, however, is not on record.
14. Registry is directed to place the report on record. 
15. We will take up claims relating to the State of Madhya Pradesh on the
next date.
16. The State of Madhya Pradesh shall also file an affidavit by Monday next
indicating therein the progress made for filling up the posts, other than the 232
posts.
DELHI
17. Ms.  Menaka  Guruswamy,  learned  senior  counsel  represents  455
(contractual) special teachers. An affidavit shall be filed on behalf of these 455
teachers indicating how many of them have been in service for more than 10
years, how many of them possess RCI qualification with up to date registration
number and how many of them have previously taken the examination for
recruitment  conducted  by  the  Delhi  Subordinate  Services  Selection  Board
(DSSSB). The engagement letters of each of these teachers shall form part of
the affidavit. 
18. The affidavit may be filed by Monday next, with a copy to the learned
amicus curiae.
19. We propose to take up the claims related to the States/Union Territories of
Jammu & Kashmir, Daman & Diu, GNCT of Delhi and Madhya Pradesh on 18 th
August, 2026, at 03:00 p.m.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.1339/2012
SABANNA & ORS.                   Appellant(s)
VERSUS
STATE OF KARNATAKA               Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. The appellant Nos.1 to 5 and 7 before us have
been convicted concurrently by both the Courts
below for the offences punishable under Sections
143, 148, 302 read with Section 149 and appellant
No.6  has  been  convicted  for  the  offences
punishable under Sections 143, 148, 302, 114 read
with Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.
Accordingly,  the  appellants  were  sentenced  to
undergo rigorous imprisonment for life. 
2. The case against the appellants is that on
09.03.2000,  the  appellants  formed  an  unlawful
assembly in the agricultural land of one Sabanna,
and committed the offences alleged using an axe
1

## Page 98

and a club, leading to the death of two persons,
namely Bhimaraya (deceased No.1) and Basavaraj
(deceased  No.2),  who  are  father  and  son
respectively.
3. Appellant No.1 is the father, and appellant
Nos.2 to 4, 6 and 7 are his children. Appellant
No.5 is the son of appellant No.6. The motive for
committing the offence is that the deceased No.1
was searching for a new bride to get his brother
Muka Hanmanth married in lieu of the strained
relationship  between  the  said  brother  and
appellant No.6, being his wife. There was an
earlier complaint lodged by deceased No.1 against
some of the appellants in respect of an occurrence
in 1991 which had resulted in the amputation of
the hand of deceased No.1. Some of the appellants
were also arrested in pursuance of the FIR lodged
then.
4. In total, the prosecution examined 18 witnesses
herein, out of which 6 of the eye-witnesses, had
turned hostile, except for PWs 1 and 3. PW-1 is
2

## Page 99

none other than the wife of deceased No.1 and the
mother of deceased No.2. PW-3 is the daughter-in-
law of deceased No.1 and the wife of deceased
No.2.
5. The Trial Court convicted the appellants by
placing reliance upon the evidence of PWs 1 and 3,
who are the eye-witnesses. On appeal, the High
Court, vide the impugned judgment, has upheld the
conviction  after  re-appreciating  the  said
evidence.
6. Learned counsel appearing for the appellants
would submit that it is unsafe to rely upon the
evidence  of  PWs  1  and  3,  being  interested
witnesses.  The  recovery  witnesses  and  the
independent witnesses have turned hostile. There
was  a  lapse  of  four  years  in  recording  the
evidence of PWs 1 and 3. Insofar as appellant No.
6 is concerned, there is a contradiction between
the evidence of PWs 1 and 3. PW-1, being the
author of the First Information Report, did not
support the case of the prosecution in speaking
3

## Page 100

about the presence of appellant No.6. Appellant
No. 5, being a juvenile, is entitled to have the
sentence set aside as he was only 16 years and
nine  months  old  at  the  time  of  the  alleged
occurrence.
7. Learned counsel appearing for the State, after
taking us through the evidence of PWs 1 and 3,
would submit that both these witnesses are natural
and have withstood the lengthy cross-examination
in support of the case of the prosecution. Though
PW-1  has  not  spoken  about  the  presence  of
appellant No.6, the same having been deposed by
PW-3, there is no need for interference with the
impugned order.
8. By placing reliance upon the affidavit filed
pursuant  to  an  earlier  order  of  this  Court,
learned counsel appearing for the State fairly
submits  that  appellant  No.5  was  admittedly  a
juvenile  at  the  relevant  point  of  time  and,
therefore, the sentence imposed upon him can be
modified accordingly, even though the said plea
4

## Page 101

had not been taken earlier. 
9. We shall first deal with the case as against
appellant No.5. The law is quite settled that the
plea of juvenility can be raised at any point of
time. As the affidavit filed by the State itself
clearly indicates the factum of appellant No.5
having been a juvenile at the time of occurrence,
we are inclined to set aside the sentence imposed
on him, while upholding the conviction rendered.
10. Accordingly, the appeal stands allowed in part
qua appellant No. 5.
11. That leaves us with the other appellants,
namely, appellant Nos.1 to 4, 6 and 7. We shall
deal with the case of appellant No.6 first.
12. As rightly submitted by the learned counsel
appearing for the appellants, PW-1, who is the
author of the First Information Report, did not
even  make  a  whisper  about  the  presence  of
appellant No.6 at the place of occurrence. The
case against appellant No.6 is that she instigated
the other accused persons to commit the offence.
5

## Page 102

In view of the apparent contradiction between the
evidence of PWs 1 and 3 with respect to the
presence of appellant No.6, it would be unsafe to
convict appellant No.6, especially when there is
no overt act attributed to her.
13. Accordingly, we are inclined to extend the
benefit of doubt to appellant No.6. In such view
of the matter, appellant No.6 stands acquitted and
the impugned judgment of the High Court confirming
the conviction rendered by the Trial Court qua
appellant No. 6, stands set aside.
14. The appeal on behalf of appellant No.6 stands
allowed, accordingly. 
15. This leaves us with the other appellants,
namely, appellant Nos.1, 2, 3, 4 and 7. On a
perusal of the evidence of PWs 1 and 3, as rightly
submitted by the learned counsel appearing for the
State, the presence of these appellants at the
scene of occurrence is not in doubt. PWs 1 and 3
have  not  only  withstood  the  lengthy  cross-
examination but have also clearly deposed on the
6

## Page 103

specific overt act attributed to these appellants.
16. An interested witness is one who is interested
in securing a conviction. The presence of PWs 1
and 3 cannot be doubted merely because they are
members of the family of the deceased. Motive,
though not relevant, also strengthens the case of
the prosecution. The fact that the evidence of PWs
1 and 3 has been recorded after a period of four
years cannot be a ground to discard them. Reliance
is placed on the decision of this Court in Baban
Shankar Daphal & Ors. v. State of Maharashtra
reported in Criminal Appeal No.1675 of 2015 in
this regard. The relevant portion of the said
decision is extracted hereinbelow:
“27.  One  of  the  contentions  of  the
learned  counsel  for  the  appellants  is
that  the  eyewitnesses  to  the  incident
were all closely related to the deceased
and for prudence the prosecution ought to
have  examined  some  other  independent
eyewitness as well who were present at
the  time  of  the  unfortunate  incident.
This was also the view taken by the Trial
Court, but the High Court has correctly
rejected such an approach and held that
7

## Page 104

merely  because  there  were  some  more
independent  witnesses  also,  who  had
reached  the  place  of  incident,  the
evidence  of  the  relatives  cannot  be
disbelieved. The law nowhere states that
the evidence of the interested witness
should be discarded altogether. The law
only warrants that their evidence should
be scrutinized with care and caution. It
has been held by this Court in the catena
of judgments that merely if a witness is
a  relative,  their  testimony  cannot  be
discarded on that ground alone.
28. In criminal cases, the credibility of
witnesses,  particularly  those  who  are
close relatives of the victim, is often
scrutinized.  However,  being  a  relative
does not automatically render a witness
"interested"  or  biased.  The  term
"interested" refers to witnesses who have
a personal stake in the outcome, such as
a  desire  for  revenge  or  to  falsely
implicate the accused due to enmity or
personal gain. A "related" witness, on
the other hand, is someone who may be
naturally present at the scene of the
crime, and their testimony should not be
dismissed  simply  because  of  their
relationship to the victim. Courts must
assess the reliability, consistency, and
coherence of their statements rather than
labelling them as untrustworthy.
29. The distinction between "interested"
and  "related"  witnesses  has  been
8

## Page 105

clarified  in  Dalip  Singh  v.  State  of
Punjab where this Court emphasized that a
close relative is usually the last person
to falsely implicate an innocent person.
Therefore, in evaluating the evidence of
a related witness, the court should focus
on  the  consistency  and  credibility  of
their  testimony.  This  approach  ensures
that the evidence is not discarded merely
due  to  familial  ties,  but  is  instead
assessed  based  on  its  inherent
reliability  and  consistency  with  other
evidence in the case. This position has
been reiterated by this Court in:
i.Md. Rojali Ali and Ors v. The State
of Assam Ministry of Home Affairs  through
secretary;
ii.Ganapathi v. State of T.N.;
iii.Jayabalan v. Union Territory of
Pondicherry.”
17. On a perusal of the impugned judgment, we find
that both the Courts have considered this aspect
in extenso. As we do not find any perversity, we
are inclined to uphold the conviction and sentence
against appellant Nos.1, 2, 3, 4 and 7.
18. We have been informed that the aforesaid
appellants  have  undergone  12  years  of
incarceration. We direct the respondent-State to
9

## Page 106

consider their case for premature release as and
when they become eligible for the same under the
relevant policy of the State.
19. Accordingly, the appeal qua appellant Nos.1 to
4  and  7  stands  dismissed  with  the  aforesaid
direction.
20. We place on record our appreciation for the
excellent  assistance  provided  by  the  learned
counsel appearing for the parties, especially the
learned counsel appearing for the State.
21. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

Criminal Appeal Nos. 653-656 of 2022 
 
 
 
 
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
Criminal Appeal Nos. 653-656 of 2022 
 
 
 
Chandu @ Chandra Shekhar Etc.   
....Appellants   
Versus 
 
The State of Madhya Pradesh  
....Respondent  
 
O R D E R  
 
An eight-year-old child was murdered and the appellants 
herein, with another person who was arrayed as A1 , were in the 
dock for murder and kidnapping with an intention to demand a 
ransom for the offences under Sections 302 and 364A of the Indian 
Penal Code, 1860 (IPC). The Special Leave Petition was filed by all 
the four accused and by order dated 13.04.2022, the SLP filed by 
the 1st petitioner; A1 (Rajesh Jain) was dismissed.  As of now, in the 
above criminal appeals,  we are only concerned with the 
implication of three others who are said to have conspired with A1 

## Page 140

Page 2 of 5 
Criminal Appeal Nos. 653-656 of 2022 
 
 
to kidnap the child for demand of ransom; the remaining 
appellants here.   
2. The death by homicide is proved by the Doctor, PW25 and 
the postmortem report produced by him. There were six injuries  
found on the body of the victim and according to the Doctor, the 
victim died of suffocation by throttling. The postmortem was done 
on 05.01.2004 at 10 o’clock  and the opinion was that  the death 
occurred less than 48 hours from the time of postmortem 
examination.  
3. We are not examining the evidence against A1; which is 
clinching and his appeal has already been rejected.  On the 
conspiracy theory the oral testimony of PWs 5, 15, 23 & 25 are 
projected. PW5 states that A1 told him about a plan to kidnap the 
boy, along with A3 and PW15 affirms that this was told to him by 
PW5. PW5 states in his chief examination that he thought it was a 
mere joke and hence did not reveal it to anybody. On the night of 
the missing of the boy being reported he told his mother and 
grandmother, is his contention , that too  on the next morning ; 
likewise, to PW15; which does not qualify as resgestae.  Then, A1 
was overheard when hatching a plan to kidnap the boy, by PW20, 

## Page 141

Page 3 of 5 
Criminal Appeal Nos. 653-656 of 2022 
 
 
the Principal and PW23, the Teacher of the School. However, it is 
quite unbelievable that a Principal and a Teacher on overhearing 
a plan to kidnap a boy, studying in their school , would not report 
the matter to the police or at least inform the boy’s family 
members. Witnesses were arrayed to speak on the pl an of 
kidnapping in which A3 was roped in but however A2 to A4 having 
not been implicated  even by any of the  said witnesses. A3’s 
involvement is said to have been spoken of by A1 , without any 
substantiation otherwise. We find absolutely no reason to sustain 
the theory of conspiracy as brought forth by the prosecution.  
4. Then, there is the ‘last seen ’ theory propounded by the 
prosecution which was sought to be proved from the testimony of 
PW1, PW3 and PW5.  PW3 spoke of having seen A1 with the victim 
before 7 o’clock walking towards the school. PW7 and PW9, the 
friends of the victim had spoken of the victim having told them that 
he would collect a tattoo from A1. There is ample evidence to show 
that A1 and the victim were in constant touch , but nothing to 
connect the other accused with the victim. PW1, however, stated 
that he saw all the accused sitting with the victim in the office 
premises of the school at 7 o’clock. However, PW5 though speaks 

## Page 142

Page 4 of 5 
Criminal Appeal Nos. 653-656 of 2022 
 
 
of having seen A2 to A4 in the office along with another person, 
whom he could not identify, he does not speak of having seen 
either A1 or the victim at the time when PW1 speaks of their 
presence together in the office premises of the school. A2 and A3 
are admittedly employed in the school. The last seen theory does 
not implicate A2 to A4 at all.  
5. The body is said to have been recovered on the information 
supplied by A1, which is not an incriminating circumstance 
against the other accused.  Recoveries are said to have been made 
from A2 to A4 which is spoken of by the Investigating Officer (I.O.) 
who was examined as PW28.  Again, we are not looking at the 
recoveries made from A1 , but those made from  disclosure of A2 
to A4 only; which were beedi & cigarette butts, peanut peels and 
a glass , from the place where they are said to have consumed 
alcohol. The recoveries made have no connection with the crime 
as such.  
6. The FSL report also speaks of blood stains being found on 
A1’s clothes. As far as A3 is concerned, it is the prosecution’s case 
that a button was recovered from the site which was similar to 
those found in the shirt recovered from A3, which also has a button 

## Page 143

Page 5 of 5 
Criminal Appeal Nos. 653-656 of 2022 
 
 
missing. There was also blood stains found in the shirt. There is 
nothing to indicate that the blood stain was of the deceased victim.  
Merely on the seizures made there can be no conviction. As we 
noticed, there was absolutely nothing recovered from A2 to  A4 
with a connection to the crime proper.  
7. We have absolutely no reason to sustain the conviction of A2 
to A4 who are already released on bail by a Coordinate Bench of 
this Court.  We make it clear that any bail bonds executed by A2 
to A4 shall stand cancelled. The criminal appeals insofar as A2 to 
A4 stands allowed, ordering their acquittal.  
8. The appeals are disposed of.    
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(S). 562-563 OF 2015
DR. MANMOHAN SINGH APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
CENTRAL BUREAU OF INVESTIGATION RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. These appeals are directed against the orders dated
16.12.2014 and 11.03.2015 passed by the Special Judge (PC
Act) (CBI)-7, Patiala House Courts, New Delhi. Vide the
above-stated  order,  the  learned  Special  Judge  took
cognizance of the offences under Sections 409 and 120-B IPC
and Sections 13(1)(c) and 13(1)(d)(iii) of the Prevention
of Corruption Act, 1988 against six persons, including the
Appellant – Late Dr. Manmohan Singh, former Prime Minister
of India.
2. It may be noticed at the outset that the CBI, after
investigation,  filed  two  closure  reports,  firstly  on
27.08.2014 and then on 21.10.2014, thereby giving a clean
chit to the Appellant.
3. Nevertheless, the learned Special Judge, for the
reasons assigned in the impugned order, turned down the
closure reports and took cognizance against the appellant.
Consequently,  vide order dated 11.03.2015, summons were
1

## Page 147

issued to him and the other co-accused persons to face
trial.
4. Ordinarily, this appeal could be disposed of as
having become infructuous due to the unfortunate demise of
the  Appellant.  We  are,  however,  informed  that  family
members of the deceased are seeking adjudication thereof on
merits. In order to appreciate whether there were good
reasons  and  sufficient  material  on  record  to  take
cognizance and consequently to summon the Appellant, we
have gone through both the closure reports filed by the CBI
with the able assistance of the learned senior counsel for
the parties.
5. Having  regard  to  the  well-known  parameters
consistently laid down by this Court in the matter of
acceptance or rejection of the final reports filed by an
investigating agency, we are satisfied that there were no
compelling reasons for the learned Special Judge to turn
down the closure reports filed by the CBI and to take
cognizance of the cited offences with respect to the
Appellant.  
6. Keeping in view the peculiar role sought to be
attributed  to  the  deceased  Appellant  in  his  official
capacity and his case being totally distinguishable, we
allow these appeals and set aside the impugned judgments
dated 16.12.2014 and 11.03.2015. We accept the closure
reports filed by the CBI and, consequently, close the
matters qua the Appellant on merits.
2

7. Ordered accordingly.
8. Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.

strenuously pointed out that having regard to the medical
condition of the petitioner and the fact that she has to
spend for her treatment and is now at the mercy of her
father, additional amount may be paid towards her medical
expenses.  In  this  regard,  learned  counsel  for  the
petitioner  pointed out to certain documents appended to
the affidavit of income and assets and liabilities which
petitioner has filed. Learned counsel for the petitioner
submitted  that  respondent  no.3/husband  has  sufficient
resources and funds to pay the petitioner a dignified
amount towards permanent alimony and this Court may not be
restrained by what is submitted by learned counsel for
respondent no.3. 
We have heard learned counsel for the respective
parties at length and on several dates prior to today’s
hearing. 
We have recorded the categorical submission made by
learned counsel for the petitioner that the petitioner is
5

## Page 158

ready and willing to accept the decree of divorce by mutual
consent.  The petitioner has also appeared through video
conferencing facility. However, there have been arguments
and counter arguments advanced with regard to the quantum
of permanent alimony that the petitioner is entitled to.
Learned counsel for the respondent(s) submitted that
respondent no.3 has positively responded to the submission
of  learned  counsel  for  the  petitioner   and  to  the
suggestions made by this Court and has increased the
quantum  of  permanent  alimony  from  Rs.15,00,000/-  to
Rs.35,00,000/-. He has to borrow certain sums of money and
is not financially well off at present. The said aspects
may be taken note of while awarding the permanent alimony
to the petitioner herein.
We have taken note of the submissions with regard to
the requirements of the petitioner and the ability of
respondent  no.3 to pay the petitioner towards permanent
alimony comparatively. We find that firstly, both parties
are agreeable to part ways and therefore to seek a decree
of  divorce  by  mutual  consent.   Secondly,  noting  the
submission of learned counsel for the respective parties,
we find that the ends of justice would be met if respondent
no.3/husband is directed to pay a sum of Rs.35,00,000/- to
the petitioner herein.  The said amount shall be paid in
6

## Page 159

the following tranches -
(a)  Rs.2,00,000/- during the course of the day; and 
(b) Rs.33,00,000/- shall be deposited before the Registry
within a period of four weeks from today or alternatively,
learned counsel for respondent no.3 is at liberty  to hand
over Demand Draft to learned counsel for the petitioner on
the said date.
List on 09.09.2026.  
It is made clear that no further arguments on the
aforesaid aspects shall be considered on the next date of
hearing.
We also take note of the cases/proceedings pending
between the parties and shall pass appropriate orders on
them, on the next date of hearing.

In case, the petitioners do not occupy the allotted

in occupying the allotted space and they have to nevertheless

who have sought to be impleaded and hence their case may also

respondents/ Mumbai Municipal Corporation has sought time to
get instructions in the matter. It was further submitted that
these are the persons who were before the Bombay  High Court.
However, they have not filed special leave petition(s) before
this Court but seek to implead themselves as petitioners.

Corporation submitted that she would get instructions in the
matter and possibly file an additional affidavit indicating 
the shop premises, if any, to be allocated to those 15 
persons also.
In the circumstances, we list this matter on 09.09.2026.

9. Applying the findings in paragraph 125 of the judgment in
the case of “ Ameesh Devgan vs. Union of India ” reported in
(2021) 1 SCC and direct that Crime/FIR No.254/2011 dated
29.05.2011 and Crime/FIR No.342/2011 which have now come to
light to be treated the statement under Section 161 of the
Code of Criminal Procedure. The Paragraph 125 of Ameesh Devgan
(supra) reads as under:-
“125. Lastly, we would also like to clarify that
Section 179 of the Criminal Procedure Code permits
prosecution of cases in the court within whose local
jurisdiction  the  offence  has  been  committed  or
consequences, have ensued. Section 186 of the Criminal
Procedure Code relates to cases where two separate g
charge-sheets have been filed on the basis of separate
FIRs and postulates that the prosecution would proceed
where the first charge-sheet has been filed on the
basis of the FIR that is first in point of time.

## Page 178

6
Principle underlying Section 186 can be applied at the
pre-charge-sheet stage, that is, post registration of
FIR  but  before  charge-sheet  is  submitted  to  the
Magistrate. In such cases ordinarily the first FIR,
that is, the FIR registered first in point of time,
should be treated as the main FIR and others as
statements under Section 162 of the Criminal Procedure
Code.  However,  in  exceptional  cases  and  for  good
reasons, it will be open to the High Court or this
Court, as the case may be, to treat the subsequently
registered FIR as the principal FIR. However, this
should  not  cause  any  prejudice,  inconvenience  or
harassment to either the victims. witnesses or the
person who is accused. We have clarified the aforesaid
position to avoid any doubt or debate on the said
aspect.”
10. We have treated this as an exceptional situation since
the original directions given in the main judgment were given
as  early  as  on  19.05.2025  and  the  Investigating  Agency
concerned  and  the  accused  have  adjusted  their  affairs
accordingly.
11. With the above observations, the IA No.131590/2026 and
miscellaneous application are disposed of.
12. Pending application(s),if any, shall also stand disposed
of.

6. The  respondent  filed  a  written  statement  in  which  inter  alia it  was
pleaded that the agreement for sale was executed in respect of house as
well as the land bearing survey no.1084/366 and, therefore, the sale
deed has been executed in accordance with the terms and conditions of

7. The trial Court on 31.01.2015 decreed the suit filed by the appellant.
Being aggrieved, the respondent preferred an appeal. The High Court by
the  impugned  judgment  dated  18.09.2025,  inter  alia,  held  that  the
appellant did not seek the relief of possession and, therefore, the suit
filed by the appellant was barred by the  proviso to  Section 34 of the
Specific  Relief  Act,  1963  (‘1963  Act’).  The  High  Court  set  aside  the
judgment and decree dated 18.09.2025 passed by the High Court and
allowed  the  appeal  preferred  by the  respondent.  Being aggrieved  the
appellant has filed this appeal.
3

## Page 188

8. Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that the High Court failed to
take note of the amended plaint which disclosed that the appellant had
sought the relief of possession which was mentioned in the cause title
and had valued the relief of possession and also paid the court fee. It is,
therefore, submitted that the impugned judgment be set aside and the
matter be remitted to the High Court for a fresh decision.
9. On the other hand, learned senior counsel for respondent submitted that
the appellant did not specifically pray for the relief of possession in the
prayer clause and, therefore, the suit filed by the appellant has rightly
been held to be non-maintainable.
10. We have perused the record and considered the submissions made on
both the sides.
11. The appellant has not specifically prayed for the relief of possession in
the prayer clause of the plaint.  On a holistic reading of the plaint and in
particular from the cause title, paragraph nos. 12A and 13 of the plaint,
it is evident that the appellant has not only prayed for the relief of
possession but has also valued the relief of possession and has paid the
court fee for the relief of possession. On account of the inadvertence on
the  part  of  the  counsel  of  the  appellant  in  drafting  the  plaint,  the
appellant  cannot  be  penalized.  In  our  opinion,  in  substance,  the
appellant  has  prayed  for the  relief  of  possession.  However,  the  High
Court failed to take note of the amended plaint and has held that the suit
to be barred by the proviso to Section 34 of the 1963 Act.
4

## Page 189

12. We, therefore, set aside the judgment dated 18.09.2025 passed by the
High Court in the First Appeal No.69 of 2015. The matter is remitted to
the High Court for decision afresh on merits. It is made clear that this
Court has not expressed any opinion on the merits of the case.
13. In view of the fact that the suit is filed way back in 2007, it would be
appropriate  to  direct  that  the  First  Appeal  must  be  taken  up  and
disposed of as expeditiously as possible, preferably within period of one
year.
14. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. However, there shall be no order as to
costs.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
    CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.       OF 2026
    (Arising out of SLP(Crl.) No.18016 of 2025)
    
ARU MEHROTRA                                  APPELLANT
                                VERSUS
ADITYA BHAN SINGH & ANR.                        RESPONDENTS
R1 : ADITYA BHAN SINGH 
R2 : THE STATE OF U.P.
O R D E R
Heard learned counsels for the parties.
2. Leave granted.
3. The present appellant seeks cancellation of bail granted to
the respondent no.1 by the High Court vide its impugned order dated
14.05.2025 in Criminal Misc. Bail Application No.2927 of 2025 in
connection with FIR No.0486 of 2024, registered at P.S. Kotwali
City, District Hardoi under Sections 61(2) and 103(1) of the
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
4. The respondent no.1 is accused of killing the father of the
complainant.
5. Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that the incident
happened due to the reason that the deceased was a tenant of the
respondent no.1 and other three persons and wanted the deceased to

## Page 204

2
vacate the premises due to which, respondent no.1 hired the killers
who executed the job. It was submitted that during investigation,
strong and cogent evidence has come to light with regard to the
direct involvement of the respondent no.1 to the crime. It was
submitted that the motorcycle on which, the assailants had come and
after the shooting had fled away, was purchased from the money
given by the respondent no.1. It was further submitted that the
Call Data Records show that the respondent no.1 was in constant
touch with the assailants and other co-accused during the relevant
period. Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that though
other landlords, who are also co-accused, have been granted bail
but in the present case, the distinction is with regard to the
purchase of  black Pulsar motorcycle on which, the assailants had
come and the Call Data Records. It was further submitted that only
after about nine months in custody, the respondent no.1 was granted
bail by the High Court. It was submitted that now the appellant,
who is the daughter of the deceased complainant, is in a very
precarious situation inasmuch as, the main shooters have also been
granted bail just because the respondent no.1 had been granted bail
in the matter and there is genuine apprehension of threat to the
appellant and her family member’s life.
6. Learned  counsel  for  the  respondent  no.2-State  of  U.P.
submitted  that  they  are  supporting  the  contentions  of  the
appellant. It was submitted that the two main witnesses, whose
testimony would link the respondent no.1 to the crime, being the
person to whom the respondent no.1 had given money for purchase of
the black Pulsar motorcycle as also the Manager of the concerned

## Page 205

3
dealer, are yet to be examined.
7. Learned counsel for the respondent no.1 submitted that all
other co-accused have been granted bail and there is no distinction
between the case of the respondent no.1 with the other co-accused.
It was further submitted that till now, there has been no evidence
brought on record during trial to link the respondent no.1 to the
crime. It was further submitted that there is also no documentary
evidence available with the prosecution to show that the black
Pulsar motorcycle used in the crime was purchased on behalf or from
the money given by the respondent no.1.
8. Having considered the matter from various angles and taking a
holistic view, we find that the impugned order granting bail to the
respondent no.1 needs interference.
9. The High Court ought to have been conscious of the fact that
there was strong and cogent material, and there were witnesses to
testify with regard to the money being given by the respondent no.1
for purchase of the motorcycle, which was used in the crime, as
also his connection to the crime based on the Call Data Records
which,  as  has  been  pointed  out  by  learned  counsel  for  the
respondent no.1-State of U.P. was brought on record by way of a
counter affidavit before the High Court but the same have not been
even referred to. Further, from the overall circumstances and
probabilities, we find that the High Court should have refrained
from granting bail to the respondent no.1 at the relevant point of
time.
10. For reasons aforesaid, the appeal is allowed. The bail granted
to the respondent no.1 by the High Court vide the impugned order

## Page 206

4
dated 14.05.2025 in Criminal Misc. Bail Application No.2927 of 2025
stands cancelled. The respondent no.1 is directed to surrender
before the Court concerned within two weeks from today.
11. Needless to say that the trial be expedited.
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

SLP (C) No.13234/2026
Non-Reportable
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.        of 2026
(Arising out of SLP (C) No.13234 of 2026) 
M/S A R RESOURCE MANAGEMENT 
CONSULTANTS          …. APPELLANT (S) 
Versus
MP ROAD TRANSPORT CORPORATION 
& ANR.               …. RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
At the outset, Sri Karthik Sundar, learned Counsel appearing for
the respondent-Corporation, submits that the respondent has also
filed  a  petition  from  the  very  same  order  impugned  herein
numbered as Diary No.44619 of 2026. We take on board the said
matter.
2. Leave granted.
3. The impugned order was passed in a petition under Article 227
of the Constitution of India which challenges the dismissal of an
Execution  Petition.  The  Execution  Petition  was  pending  for  more
than  10  years  and  the  appellant-decree  holder  had  repeatedly
remitted  the  process  fee  to  take  out  service,  which    was  not
responded to by the judgment debtor. Eventually at one instance, on
1

## Page 210

SLP (C) No.13234/2026
Court’s  directions  when  the  process  fee  was  not  remitted,  the
Execution Petition was dismissed, which led to the petition under
Article 227 of the Constitution of India. 
4. We heard Sri  Navin Pahwa, learned Senior Counsel appearing
for the appellant and Sri  Karthik Sundar, learned Counsel appearing
for the respondent-Corporation.
5. The appellant’s contention  is that in  a  petition  filed  by  the
decree holder before the High Court, a prejudicial order was passed
directing the amount deposited by the judgment debtor to be not
disbursed till the disposal of the Arbitration Appeal. The Arbitration
Award was against the Corporation, and it had unsuccessfully filed
an appeal under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act,
19961. Now the matter is pending before the High Court itself in an
appeal under Section 37 of the Act.
6. It was noticed by the High Court itself that the Corporation had
earlier deposited a sum of Rs.3,83,00,000/- (Rupees Three crore and
eighty three lakh) before the Executing Court which was disbursed
to the appellant. Learned Senior Counsel for the appellant submitted
that the said disbursal was on the appellant furnishing security to
the satisfaction of the Executing Court.
1  Hereinafter referred to as ‘the Act’
2

## Page 211

SLP (C) No.13234/2026
7. Before the High Court, the Managing Director produced a draft
of Rs.3,32,31,838/- (Rupees Three crore thirty two lakh thirty one
thousand eight hundred and thirty eight) which was directed to be
remitted before the Executing Court after restoring the executing
proceedings.  
8. Especially considering the long pendency, we are of the opinion
that  the  amount  deposited  in  the  Executing  Court  has  to  be
necessarily  disbursed  to  the  decree  holder  which  shall  be  done
within  a  period  of  two  weeks  from  today  on  the  decree  holder
producing security to the satisfaction of the Executing Court. Sri
Navin Pahwa, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellant,
further submits that already sufficient security has been provided. If
the security furnished covers the amount  which is now directed to
be disbursed, the Executing Court need not insist for any further
security.
9. The  appeal  by  the  Corporation  is  with  respect  to  the
observations in Paragraph 8. The Division Bench of the High Court
has  noticed  the  conduct  of  the  Corporation,  a  public  body,  and
deprecated  the  same  in  the  strongest  terms.  A  reading  of  the
impugned order would indicate that even before the High Court,
despite  repeated  notices,  the  Corporation  did  not  appear  and
3

## Page 212

SLP (C) No.13234/2026
eventually the Additional Advocate General was directed to inform
the Managing Director of the Corporation that if appearance is not
made, arrest warrant will be issued. We cannot observe that there
was callous indifference to the process of the court, but considering
the fact that the High Court has directed the responsibility to be
fixed on the officers concerned, we expunge  only that particular
observation.
10. The  Appeals  are  allowed  with  the  above  directions  and
observations.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

O R D E R
1. This petition under Section 11(5), Section 11(6) and Section
11(9) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (1996 Act),
seeks the appointment of a sole arbitrator to adjudicate disputes
arising from an Agreement to Sell dated 09.02.2013 (Agreement),
executed between the Petitioner and the Respondent Nos. 1 to 6 in
respect of Flat No. 4D10 in the residential apartment project
“Shanders Dwellington” at Chikkanagamangala Village, Bengaluru.
2. Briefly  stated,  the  Petitioner  is  an  Indian  national
habitually residing in Bellevue, Washington State, United States of
America. Respondent No. 1 is a company incorporated in India,
having its registered office at Bengaluru, Karnataka, and is
engaged in the business of real-estate development. Respondent Nos.
2 to 5 are the landowners of the property bearing Sy. No. 30/1A1A3
(Old Sy. No. 30/1A1A, earlier identified as Sy. No. 30) measuring 3
acres 20 guntas situated at Chikkanagamangala Village, Sarjapura
Hobli, Anekal Taluk, Bengaluru. The landowners entered into a Joint
1

## Page 226

Development Agreement dated 09.11.2009 with Respondent No. 6 (who
is the erstwhile Developer), and by registered Assignment Deed
dated 29.11.2011 the development rights were assigned to Respondent
No. 1, which was authorised under a General Power of Attorney to
develop the project and to sell the developer’s share, including
the said flat, to purchasers such as the Petitioner.
3. It appears that a dispute arose when the Petitioner sought
completion of the construction, execution of the sale deed and
handover of possession of the schedule flat in terms of the
Agreement.  It is alleged that, despite the Petitioner having made
payments towards the total sale consideration of Rs. 42,80,000/- in
accordance with the agreed milestones, Respondent No. 1 neither
handed over possession of the said Flat nor executed the sale deed
within the stipulated period. The Agreement contemplated completion
and delivery by December, 2015 with a grace period which expired in
June, 2016. In these circumstances, the Petitioner issued a legal
notice dated 29.02.2024 calling upon Respondent No. 1 to comply
with their obligations. Upon failure of the Respondent No. 1 to do
so, the Petitioner sought to initiate arbitral proceedings in
accordance with Clause 20.2 of the Agreement, which provides for
reference of disputes to a Sole Arbitrator to be appointed by the
Developer.
4. Consequently, the Petitioner issued a communication dated
13.08.2024 to Respondent No. 1, invoking the arbitration clause and
2

## Page 227

suggested the name of Justice V. Jagannathan, former Judge of the
High Court of Karnataka, for appointment as the Sole Arbitrator.
However, Respondent No. 1 objected to the arbitration as well as to
the suggested arbitrator. It is thus evident that the parties’
attempt  at  amicable  settlement  of  the  issue  of  arbitrator
appointment has also failed. Hence, the Petitioner has filed the
instant Petition under Section 11 of the 1996 Act.
5. We have heard learned Counsel for the parties, and perused the
material placed on record.
6. Keeping in view the facts and circumstances recorded above and
the relevant provision(s) under the Agreement, we deem it just and
appropriate to allow the instant Arbitration Petition and appoint
Shri Veeranna G. Tigadi, former District and Sessions Judge from
the State of Karnataka, as the Sole Arbitrator to resolve the
subsisting disputes between the parties.
7. All the objections raised by the Petitioner as well as the
Respondents  are  left  open  to  be  urged  before  the  learned
Arbitrator. The seat and venue of arbitration, in accordance with
the arbitration agreement, shall be Bangalore, India. 
8. The  Arbitrator  shall  have  the  liberty  to  fix  his  own
remuneration/fees  in  consultation  with  the  parties.  Ordered
accordingly.

2014 passed by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh, Bench at
1

## Page 236

Gwalior in S.A. No.204 of 2013.  By the said order, the
High Court has refused to condone the delay of 6965 days
in filing the Second Appeal by the State of Madhya
Pradesh.  The Second Appeal itself was filed against the
judgment and decree dated 8 th April, 1994 passed by the
Court of the First Additional District Judge, Morena,
Madhya Pradesh in Property Appeal No.41A of 1982.  The
said judgment, in turn, confirmed the judgment and decree
dated 22nd July, 1982 passed by the Court of Civil Judge,
Class II, Sablagarh, District Morena, Madhya Pradesh in
Civil Suit No.6A of 1979.  The said suit was filed by the
petitioner/plaintiff herein for permanent injunction to
stop the respondents from making further construction and
also for mandatory injunction to remove the construction
already made.
2. When this matter came up on last occasion, we
wanted the State to file a brief note explaining the
reasons for the huge delay of 19 years in filing the
Second Appeal against the judgment and decree of the
First Appellate Court dated 8th April, 1994.  
3. Ms. Manisha T.Karia, learned Additional Advocate
General appearing for the petitioner-State has today
handed over a written note wherein it is set out as
under:
a) That a committee headed by the Chief Secretary
was constituted to examine the reasons for the delay;
2

## Page 237

b) That the Committee observed that during the
period from 8 th April, 1994 to 8 th October, 2012, there
were  a total  of 17  Tehsildars (OIC)  who were  held
responsible for the delay in filing the Second Appeal;
c) That out of 17 Tehsildars, 10 have already
retired  and  under  the  Madhya  Pradesh  Civil  Services
(Pension)  Rules,  1976,  particularly,  Rule  9,  action
cannot be taken against them;
d) Out of the remaining 7 Tehsildars, 6 have
become Deputy Collectors and one remained as a Tehsildar;
and,
e) That Show Cause Notice has been issued to the
six Deputy Collectors and the one who continued to remain
as Tehsildar.
4. It has also been averred that so far as the delay
in filing the present petition is concerned, Show Cause
Notice  has  been  issued  to  two  Deputy  Collectors.
Further, 2 Tehsildars were also identified for causing
delay in filing the SLP and Show Cause Notice was also
issued to them by the office of Commissioner, Chambal
Division and the General Administration Department. It is
stated by Ms. Manisha T karia, learned senior counsel for
the petitioner that one Clerk has been suspended with
immediate effect and Show Cause Notice has been issued to
two Clerks.
3

## Page 238

5. According to the note, in all, action has been
taken  against  Deputy  Collectors,  3  Tehsildars  and  3
Clerks.
6. What is significant to note is that no details
whatsoever of the dates when the Show Cause Notices were
issued or as to the follow up action taken on such
notices has been set out.  The note is completely silent
on  whether  the  Show  Cause  Notice  resulted  in  any
departmental inquiry and, if so, whether any report was
submitted by the Inquiry Officer and further whether any
disciplinary action was taken.
7. The State is adopting a very casual approach in
this matter.  Not only was the Second Appeal delayed by
19 years, the present petition has been filed with a
delay of 826 days.  We direct the State through the
Secretary, Department of Revenue, to file a detailed
affidavit explaining as to the consequential steps that
have been taken, pursuant to the Show Cause Notice issued
to the Deputy Collectors, Tehsildars and Clerks.
8. The  Secretary,  Department  of  Revenue,  in  the
affidavit,  will  also  explain  what  according  to  the
State’s interpretation was the nature of the grant in
favour of the Pujari/Lal Kishan with regard to the suit
land.  Further, if according to the State, the Pujari/Lal
Kishan without any right or authority transferred the
4

disputed land to the predecessors of the respondents
herein Shri Fateh Chand, what consequential steps the

September, 2026. 
10. The respondents herein may file a response to the
affidavit on or before 21st September, 2026.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.10175 OF 2026
[ @ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (C) No. 27302 OF 2026 ]
[ @ DIARY NO.48823 OF 2025 ]
Deputy Commissioner of Income Tax,
CPC & Ors.
…Appellants
Versus
M/s Om Siddhakala Associates                                             
…Respondent
O R D E R
Delay condoned. Leave granted.
2. The  appeal  is  from  an  order  in  the  Writ  Petition,  which
remanded the matter to be considered afresh.
3. We  heard  learned  Standing  Counsel  appearing  for  the
Department and learned Counsel for the respondent. While learned
Counsel for the Department submits that the demand raised was in
accordance with the returns filed. Without filing a revised return, the
demand was challenged under Section 264 of the Income T ax Act,
19611,  which  when  dismissed,  the  respondent-assessee  had
approached the High Court. The claim raised could not have been
made especially, since there was no revision of returns filed by the
assessee. The learned Counsel for the assessee on the other hand
submits that the impugned order is a mere remand made and all
contentions could be raised before the appropriate authority.
4. We  are  not  convinced  that  the  remand,  in  the  facts  and
1 For brevity, ‘the Act’

## Page 246

2
circumstances  of  the  case,  was  permissible.  Admittedly,  on  self-
assessment, a return was filed by the assessee which was processed
by  the  Centralised  Processing  Centre,  Income  T ax  Department,
Bengaluru  and  a  notice  was  issued  under  Section  143(1)  and  a
subsequent notice under Section 156, demanding the outstanding
tax as coming out from the returns filed on self-assessment. The
respondent filed a revision invoking Section 264 of the Act before
the Principal Commissioner of Income T ax, who rejected the same on
the ground that there was unexplained delay, the tolerance limits as
coming out from Section 43CA were only prospective and that by
side-wind the attempt is to revise the return, after the period had
expired, by invoking Section 264.
5. The  issue  of  tolerance  limit  was  not  raised  in  the  self-
assessment  nor  was  the  assessment  revised  within  the  time
provided. The High Court, hence, fell in error, insofar as the remand
made. The assessee having not claimed the same in the returns filed
could have revised the return within the time provided under the
Act. When that was not done, there is no question of revision under
Section 264, which would be an attempt to revise the return under
the garb of a revision.
6. Learned  Counsel  for  the  respondent-assessee  submits  that
there has been re-assessment made after remand. Necessarily, if

## Page 247

3
the remand order is set aside, the order passed on re-assessment
will also have no effect, being a dependent order. We hence set
aside  the  impugned  judgment  of  the  High  Court  and  as  a
consequence any re-assessment made would not be applicable. The
assessee would have to pay tax on the basis of the returns filed on
which an intimation was issued and a demand raised.
7. The appeal is allowed to that extent clearly observing that we
have not entered into the question of whether the tolerance limit
would be retrospective or prospective.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
    CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.       OF 2026
    (Arising out of SLP(Crl.) No.14259 of 2025)
    
ABHINAV VERMA                                   APPELLANT
                                VERSUS
STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH & ANR.                      RESPONDENTS
R1 : STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH
R2 : DILEEP VERMA
O R D E R
Heard learned senior counsel/counsels for the parties.
2. Leave granted.
3. The appellant-complainant is aggrieved by grant of bail to
respondent no.2 by the High Court vide its impugned order dated
15.07.2025 in Criminal Misc. Bail Application No.1888 of 2025 in
connection with FIR No.0626 of 2024 dated 11.10.2024, registered at
P.S. Kotwali, Akbarpur, District Ambedkar Nagar for the offence
under Section 308(4) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
4. Learned counsel for the appellant-complainant submitted that
the respondent no.2, who is a habitual criminal, had given death
threats to the appellant and his family members if the extortion
demanded by him was not paid. It was submitted that in the past
also, such extortion was demanded and due to the intervention of a

## Page 251

2
common  acquaintance,  the  matter  was  settled.  It  was  further
submitted that the respondent no.2 has at least fifty-one other
criminal antecedents that too under major Sections of various penal
statutes for murder, attempt to murder, possessing and using arms
etc. Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that under such
background, grant of bail to the respondent no.2, who has spent
only about six and a half months behind bars, was not justified.
5. Learned counsel for the respondent no.1-State of Uttar Pradesh
has adopted the arguments advanced by the learned counsel for the
appellant.
6. Learned senior counsel for the respondent no.2 submitted that
the Court should look only into the allegations in the present case
and the Section under which, the respondent no.2 has been charged
which is triable by a Magistrate and the discretion exercised by
the High Court ought not to be interfered with. It was submitted
that in most of the cases, either the respondent no.2 has been
acquitted or has been on bail.
7. Having considered the matter in its entirety, we find that a
case for interference has been made out.
8. The first and foremost principle relating to grant of bail is
the overall preponderance of circumstances and also the issue
whether the person who would be granted bail deserves to be set
free in the background of his past conduct, that is, of repeatedly
committing offences one after the other.
9. In the present case, we find that respondent no.2 has a
chequered history and has cases pending against him for more than
two decades. Equally to be noted is the fact that respondent no.2

## Page 252

3
has been charged for crimes, which are serious and heinous in
nature and in one of the crimes, he has also been convicted by the
Trial Court and sentenced for life imprisonment, though he is
presently on bail during the pendency of his appeal before the High
Court.
10. For reasons aforesaid, the appeal is allowed. The bail granted
to the respondent no.2 by the High Court vide its impugned order
dated 15.07.2025 in Criminal Misc. Bail Application No.1888 of 2025
stands cancelled. The respondent no.2 is directed to surrender
before the Court below, latest within two weeks from today.
11. Needless to say that the trial be expedited.
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. A suit for specific performance by the petitioner
herein was decreed. The respondent who was the defendant in
the suit filed an appeal and the petitioner deposited
balance  sale  consideration  of  Rs.35,00,000/-  (Rupees
Thirty-five lakh) as per the order of the court.

## Page 256

2. The  appeal  was  dismissed  for  non-prosecution  on
15.11.2023 and there was a restoration application brought
on record on 03.11.2025 with a delay of 689 days. The
Appellate  Court  rejected  the  application  finding  no
satisfactory reason for the delay occasioned.
3. The High Court condoned the delay which is impugned in
the above Special Leave Petition.
4. Learned Senior Counsel for the petitioner pointed out
that there is gross delay with no satisfactory explanation.
It is also pointed out that the entire balance sale
consideration  has  been  deposited  before  the  Appellate
Court.
5. Learned Counsel for the respondent argued to sustain
the  order,  especially  since  the  relief  for  specific
performance is a discretionary one, and on hardship found,
there could always be a refund order without divesting the
owner of the property.
6. The High Court has recorded the reasons as stated in
the affidavit. The appellant-defendant claimed that both
the Advocate and the defendant had fallen sick between
November 2023 and August 2024. The defendant is said to
have been afflicted with viral fever; quite difficult to
believe that it continued for more than a year. As far as

## Page 257

the delay occasioned from August 2024, it was explained
that a defective application was filed in August 2024
itself, but after return, it was misplaced in the office of
the Advocate.
7. We do not find any reason, having been projected,
which could have persuaded the High Court to allow the
restoration, without any terms.
8. We are of the opinion that the appeal could be
restored on terms, which we fix at Rs.50,000/- (Rupees
Fifty thousand) as costs on the respondent herein, who is
the appellant before the First Appellate Court.
9. The respondent shall pay the above costs or deposit it
before the First Appellate Court within a period of 3 weeks
from today and if paid directly, a memo shall be produced
within the period stipulated.
10. On such costs being paid or deposited, the appeal
shall stand revived. Considering the fact that the appeal
is of the year 2023, we request the First Appellate Court
to expedite the hearing, especially since considerable
amount  as  balance  sale  consideration  is  said  to  be
deposited before Court.
11. With the above directions, we dispose of the Special

## Page 258

Leave Petition.
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

refunded, returnable after four weeks. 
Mr. S. Nagamuthu, learned Senior Counsel, assisted by
learned Advocate-on-Record, who is on caveat, accepts and
waives formal notice on behalf of Respondent Nos.1,3 & 4.
We are informed by the learned Senior Counsel that
Respondent No.2 is no more alive.
In view of the above, the name of Respondent No.2 is
ordered to be deleted from the array of respondents.
Cause title be amended accordingly.
Learned  Senior  Counsel  shall  have  instructions
regarding  refund  of  the  earnest  money  to  the
petitioner on the next date of hearing.”
3. Thus, the notice was issued on the limited point as to why
the earnest money paid by the petitioner be not ordered to be
refunded.
4. We heard the learned counsel appearing for the parties.
5. We looked into the judgment of the Trial Court as well as
the well reasoned judgment of the High Court.  The High Court
after  due  consideration  of  the  materials  on  record  has
2

## Page 277

recorded a categorical finding that the agreements of sale
purported to have been executed by the respondents in favour
of the appellant before us (original plaintiff) are bogus.
6. If that be so, then in our opinion, there is no question
of asking the respondents (original defendants) before us to
refund the earnest money.
7. With the aforesaid, the appeal is dismissed.
8. Pending application(s), if any, stands disposed of.

We  have  heard  the  learned  Senior  Counsel
appearing for the appellant and Mr. S.V. Raju,
learned ASG appearing for the respondent(s).
Though the learned counsel appearing for the
parties seek to argue on merits, we take note of the
order passed by a three Judges Bench of this Court
dated 19.09.2024 which reads as follows:
“The learned senior counsel appearing for
the appellant states that the appellant would
like  to  apply  for  clarification  of  the
judgment dated 11 th September, 2023 of the
Full  Bench  in  the  case  of  CBI  v.  R.R.
Kishore.
Hence, list on 27th November, 2024.
We make it clear that this Court has not
stayed the proceedings of trial.”
Mr.  Arvind  Datar,  learned  Senior  Counsel
appearing for the appellant, would submit that he
may  be  permitted  to  file  an  application  for
clarification in this regard.
Accordingly, learned Senior Counsel appearing
for  the  appellant  is  permitted  to  file  an
appropriate application for clarification.

## Page 297

3
The incidental question, which again is raised
by the learned Senior Counsel, is on the composition
of the Bench.
In our considered view, the order passed by the
three Judges Bench dated 19.09.2024 referred above
would mean that the said clarification application
has to be decided by a five Judges Bench alone.
Learned Senior Counsel further submits that it
would be difficult for the appellant to seek the
constitution of such a Bench.
Taking note of the said submission, as and when
such  an  application  is  filed,  the  Registry  is
directed to place the same before Hon’ble the Chief
Justice of India fo r listing b efore a five Judges
Bench, in view of our understanding of the order
dated 19.09.2024, especially when the clarification
sought for is with respect to the order passed by a
five Judges Bench.
Learned counsel appearing for the appellant is
permitted  to  file  a  fresh  application,
notwithstanding the fact of an earlier application
having been filed.
Accordingly,  IA  No.261739/2024  in  Criminal
Appeal No.3063/2023, st ands closed with liberty to
the appellant to file a fresh application.

b) No FSL report, fingerprint examination

tainted  currency  notes  were  conducted  to

proceedings despite the trap being laid in the

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
CIVIL APPEAL  NO(S).  10037-10038 OF 2026
[@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (C) Nos. 27427-27428 OF 2023]
M/S KARUNYA EDUCATIONAL TRUST                  Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
M/S CHINMAYA GARDEN TRUST & ORS.              Respondent(s)
O R D E R 
1. Leave granted.
2. These appeals are directed against the order
dated 28.06.2023 passed by the High Court in CRP Nos.
4380 and 4381 of 2015, by which the High Court has
allowed the petitions filed by the respondents and set
aside the order passed by the Trial Court, by which it
had rejected the application under Order VII Rule 11
of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 [“the Code”].
3. The facts giving rise to filing of these appeals
are that the appellant had filed a suit seeking
declaration  of  title,  partition  and  consequential
reliefs in respect of the suit schedule properties.
The respondents filed an application under Order VII
Rule 11 of the Code seeking rejection on the ground
that the same is barred by res judicata.  The Trial
Court, by an order dated 10.08.2015, rejected the
application under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code on the
ground that the issue requires adjudication after
recording of the evidence and cannot be decided by

## Page 324

2
means of an application under Order VII Rule 11 of the
Code.
4. Being aggrieved, the respondents filed a Revision
before the High Court.  The High Court, by impugned
order  dated  28.06.2023,  allowed  the  revision  and
rejected the plaint.
5. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant
and the respondents at length and perused the record.
From the perusal of the order passed by the High
Court, it is evident that the High Court, while
deciding the Revision, has travelled beyond the plaint
and  has  looked  into  the  documents  filed  by  the
respondents along with the application under Order VII
Rule 11 and proceeded to record a finding that the
appellant does not hold a valid title, as the same has
been earlier adjudicated in the Partition Suit, namely
O.S. No. 517 of 1992.
6. It is well-settled in law that while deciding 
an application under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code,
the court can only look into the averments of plaint
and cannot consider other documents. In the instant
case, the High Court while deciding the application
under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code considered the
documents filed by the respondents. 
7. For  the  aforementioned  reasons,  the  impugned
order passed by the High Court is set aside. The civil
suit  filed  by  the  appellant  is  restored  to  its

## Page 325

3
original number. The Trial Court, on the basis of the
pleadings  of  the  parties,  shall  frame  issues,
including the issue on maintainability of the suit on
the ground of res judicata and shall proceed to decide
the suit.
8. Since the suit dates back to 2013, we direct the
Trial Court to decide the same as expeditiously as
possible, preferably within a period of one year from
today.  Accordingly, the civil appeals are allowed.
9. Pending  interlocutory  application(s),  if  any,
is/are disposed of.

rape  and  circulation  of  compromising  photographs.  On
investigation it was also found that, the petitioner was
operating and maintaining Instagram accounts in which the
photos were uploaded.
4. The Investigating Officer was also present in court, with
whom we interacted. We specifically put a query to him as
to  the  nature  of  the  photos,  alleged  to  have  been
circulated. We showed him the photographs produced by the
petitioner in a sealed cover, which he affirms were the
photographs circulated. The photographs only show both the
petitioner and the alleged victim together. 
5. We find that the allegation itself is that the victim got
acquainted with the petitioner in the year 2019, and the
FIR is of the year 2025. Admittedly, now the victim is a
major. The chargesheet has been filed in May 2026, and
there is no progress in the trial.
6. On a prima facie consideration of the material on record,
we are of the opinion that the petitioner can be released
SLP(Crl.)  No.11115/2026 3

## Page 330

on bail, subject to such terms and conditions that the
Sessions Judge, Gautam Buddha Nagar (the jurisdictional
court) may deem fit to impose. Ordered accordingly. One of
the conditions shall be that, the petitioner shall not
enter Noida or Delhi, unless his presence is required in
the Court, for continuation of the trial. The petitioner
shall cooperate with the trial, and shall remain present
before the Trial Court, as and when directed.  
7. With the above directions, the Special Leave Petition is
disposed of. 
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed
of.

JAINI SINGH                                    APPELLANT
                                VERSUS
STATE OF U.P.                                       RESPONDENT
O R D E R
Heard learned senior counsel/counsel for the parties.
2. Leave granted.
3. Earlier while issuing notice on 16.01.2026, we have recorded
the following:-
 “At  the  outset,  learned  Senior  Counsel  for  the
petitioner submits that the petitioner was convicted for
life imprisonment by the trial court, which had been
modified to 14 years R.I. by the High Court vide the
impugned order dated 26.11.2025 passed in Criminal Appeal
No.7008 of 2011 and analogous cases. 
2. It was submitted that in view of the serious ailment
suffered by the petitioner, who is 80 years of age and
suffering from kidney and liver diseases, he was granted
exemption from surrendering by the learned Chamber Judge
on 05.01.2026 till today i.e. till the date of first
listing before the Court.
3. Thus, learned counsel submitted that the incident being
of the year 1993, the Court may consider interfering with
the quantum of sentence as the petitioner had already
undergone custody for close to 10 years.
4.  Issue  notice.  In  the  meantime,  exemption  from
surrendering to continue till the next date of listing.
5. List on 14.04.2026.”
4. Learned senior counsel for the appellant submitted that the
only role attributed to the appellant is that he was also a part of

## Page 332

2
a mob and though he had a stick in his hand, the allegation is that
the entire mob assaulted the deceased persons. It was further
contended  that  no  specific  role  has  been  attributed  to  the
appellant by any of the witnesses. He reiterates his earlier
submission that the appellant is almost eighty years old suffering
from serious kidney and liver diseases and has been in actual
custody for nine years and ten months.
5. Learned counsel for the respondent-State of Uttar Pradesh
submits that the appellant was very much an active part of the mob
and cannot be said to be innocent and he had a common object in
furtherance of which, he also participated in an overt-act of
assault by  lathi leading to the death of three persons. It was
further submitted that earlier, the prayer for remission of the
appellant was considered by the respondent-State of U.P. and
benefit was given but the complainant had moved to the High Court
leading to cancellation of the said order by the High Court, which
has been upheld by this Court vide order dated 30.07.2021 in
SLP(Crl.) No.5453 of 2021.
6. Having considered the matter in its entirety and particularly,
the fact that the appellant is eighty years old having serious
ailments, we are persuaded to interfere in the quantum of sentence.
As the sentence has been modified by the High Court from Section
302/149 to that of Section 304 (Part-I) of the Indian Penal Code,
1860 (for short, the “IPC”) where the minimum sentence which can be
awarded is ten years extending to life imprisonment, we feel that
the interest of justice would be served by reducing the period of
sentence to ten years.

## Page 333

3
7. Accordingly, the appeal stands partly allowed by upholding the
conviction and reducing the sentence awarded to the appellant from
life imprisonment to ten years of actual incarceration.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

Class II, Punalur in Calendar Case No.161 of 2001 convicting the
appellant under Sections 27(1)(e) III and IV of the Kerala Forest
Act, 1961 (for short, the “Act”) and sentencing him to undergo

months under Section 27(1)(e) III of the Act, and to undergo simple

under Section 27(1)(e)IV of the Act as upheld by the learned
Sessions Court, Kollam, has been dismissed.
4. On the last occasion, we had indicated to the learned counsel
for the parties as to whether the matter can be compounded in terms
of the statutory provisions.
5. Today, learned counsel for the respondent-State of Kerala
informs that in terms of Section 68 of the Act, the present matter
can be compounded.
6. On a further query with regard to the terms, it is submitted
that the appellant shall have to pay an amount of Rs.30,200/-
(Rupees Thirty Thousand Two Hundred).
7. Learned counsel for the appellant readily agrees for the
amount and he submits that it shall be paid within eight weeks from
today.
8. Having considered the matter, we are persuaded to interfere in
the impugned order.
9. Accordingly, the offence alleged against the appellant under
Sections 27(1)(e) III and IV of the Act stands compounded, subject
to payment of Rs.30,200/- (Rupees Thirty Thousand Two Hundred)
within eight weeks from today.
10. The proceedings stand concluded and the appellant stands
discharged from the case.

Usually, in a challenge to the proceedings under
the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the deposit will be
50 per cent. Furthermore, in the case at hand, the
appellant(s) have preferred an appeal before the
High Court.
On facts, it is not in dispute that the appeal
is pending consideration.
In such view of the matter, we modify the order
passed by the High Court to the effect that the
appellant(s) shall deposit the 50 per cent of the

appellant(s), in pursuant to our order passed today.

appellant(s) to oppose such an application.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Heard Mr. Gaurav Agarwal ,  learned senior counsel for the
petitioners/applicants.
2. For the reasons stated in the accompanying affidavit, the I.A.
No. 45737/2026 is allowed and the Civil Appeal is restored to its
original file and number.
3. Accordingly, the Miscellaneous Application stands disposed of.
4. We have heard Mr. Gaurav Agarwal, learned senior counsel for

## Page 380

2
the appellants and Mr. Manish Kumar, learned Advocate-on-Record for
the respondents.
5. The appellants assailed the judgment dated 05.09.2008, passed
in Letters Patent Appeal No. 330 of 1999 1 by the High Court. The
LPA was filed questioning the order in Writ Petition bearing
C.W.J.C. No. 4523 of 1989 dated 14.12.1998 passed by the Single
Judge of the High Court. The issue arises under the  Bihar Land
Reforms (Fixation of Ceiling Area and Acquisition of Surplus Land)
Act, 19612. The declarant was granted, along with his three sons,
four independent units. The challenge of the declarant is for the
grant  of  three  additional  independent  units  to  the  family
consisting of the declarant and his sisters. The basis for such a
claim emanates from the circumstance that the father of the
declarant and his sisters, ‘C. Das’ died in the year 1957.
Therefore, with the demise of the father, the succession opened and
the brother and sisters have become entitled to their respective
shares in the property left behind by late ‘C. Das’. The appellants
have placed before the Court a xerox copy of the death certificate
which has not been considered and accepted in favour of the
appellants. Secondly, this is a claim by each one of the persons
entitled to determination and allocation of the land left behind by
late ‘C. Das’. Admittedly, it has been the declarant who is alone
fighting for the entitlement of his sisters. The impugned judgment
refers to this unavailable ground to the appellant and observes
that this circumstance is also not well founded inasmuch as if at
1 Hereinafter referred to as ‘LPA’.
2 For short,‘the Act’.

## Page 381

3
all the entitlement of sisters of declarant is taken note of.
Similarly, the property held by the husbands of his sisters should
also be taken note of. 
6. For want of the details on this behalf, this contention is
also rejected.
7. Having regard to the findings of fact recorded, we see no
reason to interfere with the order(s) impugned.
8. The appeal is, accordingly, dismissed.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
    (LOKESH ARORA)                              (NIDHI MATHUR)
SENIOR PERSONAL ASSISTANT                     COURT MASTER (NSH)

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.         OF 
(ARISING OUT OF SLP (CIVIL) NO. 12407 OF 2025)
AMIT TALWAR APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
EMAAR INDIA LIMITED & ORS. RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. In Consumer Complaint No.459/2017 filed by the predecessor-in-
interest of the appellant before the National Consumer Disputes
Redressal Commission (NCDRC), the following reliefs were sought:
“(i)Allow the present complaint;
{ii)Opposite party no.1 be directed to pay Rs.63,30,607.15
for delay in possession of the Impugned property;
(iii)  The opposite party no.1 is directed to compensate
the  complainant  of  Rs.10,00,000/-  towards  mental
harassment, frustration and agony;
(iv)  The opposite party no.1 be directed to-compensate
the complainant of Rs.5,00,000/- towards litigation costs
and other expenses; and
(v) Any other relief that this Hon’ble Forum may deem fit
in the facts and circumstances of the case and in the
interest of justice.”
3. The said complaint was allowed in part in the following terms:
“(i) opposite party shall pay compensation for the delay
in  handing  over  possession  to  the  complainant  from
25.12.2012, the date committed in the Agreement for the
same  till  05.03.2018,  the  date  of  actual  offer  of
possession, at the rate of 9% simple interest per annum;
(ii) this amount shall be paid within eight weeks of this
1

## Page 410

order, failing which the rate of interest shall be 12%
p.a.
(iii)  opposite party shall pay litigation costs of
Rs.50,000/- to the complainant.”
4. In the execution proceedings, the respondent-developer raised
an additional claim of non-payment of the full amount of allotment
price, and that has been accepted by the NCDRC vide the impugned
order to the extent that the respondent has been permitted to set-
off a total sum of Rs.15,77,630/- along with simple interest @ 15%
p.a. from 30.06.2017 to 09.08.2024.  The aggrieved appellant has
approached this Court.
5. As may be seen from the operative part of the original order
of the NCDRC, which amounts to a decree in favour of the appellant,
no  set-off  claim  was  accepted  or  granted  in  favour  of  the
respondent.  That being so, in the execution proceedings, the NCDRC
could not have gone beyond the decree. The appeal is, therefore,
allowed. The impugned order is set aside, and the respondent is
directed to comply with the original order of the NCDRC within a
period of one month.
........................CJI.

against  an  interim  order  passed  by  the
Division  Bench  of  the  High  Court  while
entertaining an intra court appeal preferred
by the respondent(s) herein.
2. It is informed by the learned senior
counsel for the petitioner that probably due
to  the  pendency  of  this  Special  Leave
Petition,  the  Division  Bench  of  the  High
Court  is  not  proceeding  ahead  with  the
hearing of the intra court appeal.
3. Considering the above, we dispose of
this Special Leave Petition requesting the
Division Bench of the High Court to decide
the pending intra court appeal between the
parties expeditiously preferably within six
months from today.
4. At this stage, learned senior counsel
for  the  petitioner  submits  that  the
petitioner  is  in  occupation  of  the
accommodation  provided  by  the  respondent-
University,  however,  the  petitioner
apprehends that her may be evicted during
pendency  of  the  respondent’s  intra  court

appeal before the High Court.
5. Considering that the matter is pending
before the Division Bench of the High Court,
we direct that the petitioner shall not be
evicted from the subject premises provided
that  the  petitioner  pays  the  occupation
charges thereof, inclusive of penal rent as
and  when  demanded  by  the  respondent-
University.
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall
stand disposed of.

         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE ARUN PALLI
For Petitioner(s) : 
                   Mr. Krunal Verma, Adv.
                   Mrs. Yugandhara Pawar Jha, AOR
